questions.questionOriginal: Tell me about the time that you had to have difficult performance conversation with your subordinate, and how you handled it, and what was the outcome?
questions.answerGiven: I am lucky to work with very talented and hard-working people, but there was one case which could be an example of difficult conversation. When I first arrived to Gentrack, I observed people first, not jumping to conclusions. I have noticed one team member, which was consistently underdelivering. Stories gets dragged from sprint to sprint, for one or another reason. I have prepared for the conversation, and took him out for a walk. During the walk I have asked how is he doing and what are the challenges. He replied, and then I said, I have observed that you are able to create much more than you're doing right now. Can you think about what stops you from doing your best work? He said that changing teams every few months was quite demotivating, along with the feeling that other team members monopolize all the interesting work. I offered him assistance with going through work and choosing bigger, more interesting features and claiming it for him, if he is able to deliver on time. Also went through team stability chances - we were going to be one team for longer period of time. Then had more heart to heart conversation about how things are at the moment. It really helped, as after that he started taking bigger and consistent features, and assist others with work much more, being active in Slack channels, etc. I think that was not easy conversation, but it helped a lot
questions.additionalDetailConfirmed: Tanya agreed that the engineer would own challenging, bounded stories such as a small feature end to end within a sprint. She followed up for two months with consistent check-ins, completed-work review and explicit feedback during every second one-to-one. He began completing one or two stories within each sprint; Tanya confirmed on 11 October 2026 that the improvement continued well beyond the two-month follow-up. Exact longer duration and baseline throughput are not established.

strengths: uses a specific and relevant management example
shows observation and curiosity before judgement
connects the intervention to visible behavioural improvement
risks: the opening delays the direct answer
the performance gap and expected standard are not stated crisply
the answer as originally delivered omitted the established follow-up cadence
allocating more interesting work could sound like rewarding underperformance unless framed as accountable ownership
efficientOutline: State the performance pattern and why it mattered
Explain that Tanya observed before concluding and prepared evidence
Describe the private conversation: direct observation, open question and root cause
Describe the agreement: meaningful ownership paired with reliable delivery expectations
Close with observable changes in ownership, consistency and team contribution
coaching.suggestedAnswer: When I joined Gentrack, I noticed one engineer's stories repeatedly carrying over between sprints. I observed the pattern before having a private conversation to understand what was getting in the way. He described demotivation from frequent team changes and limited access to interesting work. We agreed that he would own challenging, bounded stories, such as a small feature, and see them through end to end within a sprint. I followed up for two months through consistent check-ins, reviewing completed work and providing explicit feedback. He began completing one or two stories within each sprint, and the improvement continued well beyond that follow-up period. This reinforced that empathy and accountability work together: understand the barriers, agree a clear expectation and follow through on actual delivery.

questions.questionOriginal: How would you describe your leadership style?
questions.answerGiven: Empathetic, finding the cause that motivates people, finding where people can do their best work. Challenging where necessary, providing clear expectations, with strong focus to assist with removing blockers to do their best work.
likelyIntent: fit with the company's management culture
ability to adapt leadership to individuals

strengths: recognises motivation and blockers as management responsibilities
mentions clear expectations rather than support alone
risks: the original answer is a list of traits rather than a clear leadership model
it gives no observable example of how the style appears in practice
the phrase finding the cause that motivates people may sound as though motivation is something a manager can manufacture
accountability and follow-through are less prominent than support
efficientOutline: Name the style: people-centred, clear and adaptable
Explain three behaviours: understand the person, establish ownership and expectations, remove blockers while following through
Give one brief proof point from current leadership
Close with the intended result for people and delivery
coaching.suggestedAnswer: I would describe my leadership style as people-centred, clear and adaptable. I invest time in understanding what motivates each person and where their strengths can create the most value, but I pair that with clear expectations, meaningful ownership and regular feedback. My role is to remove systemic blockers and provide support, while still challenging people and following through on commitments. In my current team, that approach has helped build stronger knowledge sharing and collaboration, while consistent check-ins have helped individuals take greater ownership of delivery. I want people to feel trusted and supported, but also to understand clearly what good performance looks like.

questions.questionOriginal: What does leadership mean to you?
questions.answerGiven: It is gentle but firm and clear guidance, also assistance.
questions.candidateReflection: Tanya felt caught off guard by the breadth of the question.
likelyIntent: distinction between leadership and task management
ability to create clarity and alignment
understanding of leadership through the success of others

strengths: recognises that leadership combines care with firmness
is consistent with Tanya's empathetic leadership evidence
risks: the answer is too abstract to reveal a leadership philosophy
guidance and assistance may imply that the leader directs and rescues rather than enabling ownership
it omits shared purpose, decision clarity, accountability and development
it does not define how success should be visible in the team
efficientOutline: Define leadership as creating conditions for collective success
Name the leader's responsibilities: purpose, priorities, decision boundaries and standards
Explain how the leader enables people: trust, coaching, blocker removal and honest feedback
Clarify that leadership builds ownership rather than dependence
Define success as a capable team delivering sustainably without needing the leader in every decision
coaching.suggestedAnswer: To me, leadership means creating the conditions in which people can do strong work together. That starts with a clear purpose, priorities, decision boundaries and an honest definition of good performance. It also means understanding people's strengths, giving them meaningful ownership, removing systemic blockers and providing direct feedback when expectations are not being met. I do not see leadership as making every decision or solving every problem for the team. It is about helping people build the confidence and judgement to act independently while knowing support is available. I consider leadership successful when the team delivers sustainably, people grow, and progress does not depend on the leader being involved in every detail.

questions.questionOriginal: Let's go through your current manager and back into the past. Supply a name and a rating from 1 to 10: if I were to contact them, how would they rate you?
questions.answerGiven: Tanya supplied manager names and ratings. She rated the likely assessment from her current manager as 7 out of 10 and continued through previous managers. She did not disclose her current conflict with her manager.

coaching.suggestedAnswer: For my current manager, I would estimate around 7 out of 10, although I would rather ground that in actual feedback than pretend the number is precise. They have recognised my empathetic people leadership, team advocacy, delegation, relationship building and proactive planning. They have also challenged me to deepen my understanding of the current product architecture, uphold delivery expectations consistently, reduce work in progress and improve estimation. I think that is a fair assessment, and I have been actively working on those areas. I can give you the same evidence-based view for previous managers. I am also happy to agree appropriate referees later in the process, but I would want any contact to happen only with my explicit confirmation.

questions.questionOriginal: What are you good at in your work? What are you not good at?
questions.answerGiven: I think I am good at finding patterns across complex systems with high uncertainty, using an accounting-postings example; I am passionate about the people I lead; I am good at developing people's careers, onboarding, and explaining until they understand at a deeper level. I am not good at challenging people too much, regularly working overtime, or working with companies without work-life balance. I wanted to be explicit about that. I believe people do their best work when they are motivated and challenged, but held to achievable expectations.
questions.additionalDetailConfirmed: Tanya explicitly said she is not good at working with people who consistently overwork, take pride in doing so, and raise the implicit performance bar for others to an unachievable level.
questions.answerCompleteness: The accounting-postings example was referenced but its details have not yet been captured.
likelyIntent: relevance of strengths to the Engineering Manager role
ability to learn and mitigate weaknesses
fit with the company's performance expectations

strengths: identifies a distinctive combination of systems thinking and people development
connects technical pattern recognition with uncertainty
shows commitment to onboarding and deep understanding rather than superficial instruction
states a clear belief in achievable expectations and sustainable performance
risks: too many strengths are listed without prioritising the most role-relevant two
not challenging people too much is ambiguous and may be heard as avoiding accountability
overtime and poor work-life balance are environmental boundaries rather than capability weaknesses
saying she is not good at working with chronic overworkers may sound like an inability to manage high performers unless she distinguishes high standards from unsustainable heroics
the answer does not explain how Tanya is improving a genuine development area
efficientOutline: Name two connected strengths: systems pattern recognition and people development
Give one short proof point for each
Name a genuine shadow side: empathy can delay an explicit challenge
Explain the management practice used to address it
State sustainable-work expectations separately as a condition for good performance, not as a weakness
coaching.suggestedAnswer: My strongest combination is systems thinking and people development. I am good at finding patterns across complex systems where the problem is uncertainâ€”for example, tracing accounting postings and connected rules until I can explain the underlying behaviour clearly. On the people side, I am particularly strong at onboarding, understanding individual strengths and helping people build deeper capability rather than simply giving them instructions. One area I have had to develop is challenging performance early enough. My instinct is to understand and support the person first, which can sometimes delay an explicit conversation about expectations. I now address that by naming the observed gap, agreeing achievable outcomes and using regular check-ins and feedback. I also care strongly about sustainable performance. I find it challenging when chronic overtime is celebrated as a virtue and becomes an implicit, unachievable standard for everyone else. I value high standards and will support exceptional effort when genuinely necessary, but I do not believe heroics should become the normal operating model or substitute for prioritisation and realistic planning.
